Extends the experiments to SO(3) molecular conformations, with approximately 175,000 training examples. Neighborhood-size studies, neighbor-purity measurements, runtime reporting, and implementation details provide useful supporting analysis.
weaknesses: The implemented estimators do not generally match the theory. Equation 2 defines an intrinsic, squared-geodesic Fréchet mean, but Appendix E substitutes the circular mean on SO(2) and an SVD-derived matrix-Fisher mode on SO(3). These are not generally equivalent. For example, angles {0°, 0°, 90°} have intrinsic mean 30° but circular mean approximately 26.57°. Proposition 3.1 therefore does not establish the claimed general consistency of the implemented pipeline.

The proof invokes conditions absent from the proposition: right-invariance of the metric and concentration within a region supporting the stated centroid-stability bound. The Tukey extension also lacks justification for consistent, canonical-independent mode selection in symmetric multimodal distributions. A common initialization does not resolve this ambiguity, and the illustrative simulations do not establish the claimed guarantee.

The explanation of partial symmetries in Appendix D.4 conflicts with the invariant architecture. Exactly rotation-related inputs have identical invariant embeddings and cannot receive distinct invariant centering predictions. Consequently, separating handwritten 6s and 9s must depend on residual shape differences or imperfect invariance; the examples do not establish the claimed ability to distinguish classes occupying the same group orbit.

The OOD experiments do not faithfully evaluate the stated likelihood mechanism. Appendix F.1.1 uses absolute centered angle, ignoring the predicted distribution width, rather than Equation 5's negative log likelihood. This matters when classes have different supports. FashionMNIST's ID/OOD labeling is also underspecified: the experiment refers to symmetry ranges, although its generating distributions are Gaussian and no cutoff is provided.

The held-out evaluation protocol needs correction. Appendix F.2.1 explicitly selects EquiAdapt and ESCNN hyperparameters using test accuracy. Although this may favor those baselines, it compromises the independence of the reported test comparisons. Hyperparameters should be selected on validation data, followed by a separate final evaluation.

Comparisons and ablations are insufficient to establish the contribution beyond standard distribution centering. SGM is identified as the closest symmetry-discovery method but receives no quantitative comparison on that task. Test-time group averaging is omitted despite being able to grant invariance to frozen predictors. Downstream comparisons between classical and Tukey centering are also missing.

The molecular accuracy criterion is poorly calibrated. For the three stated target matrices, the constant prediction F = (100.002/3)I achieves entrywise MSE approximately 741 for every target, already below the paper's approximately 800 cutoff for 'accurate' predictions. Thus, the claim that roughly 80% of molecules are accurately recovered needs stronger evidence, including constant baselines and distribution-level metrics.

The experimental scope is narrower than the broad claims suggest. All pose distributions are synthetically imposed; molecular conformers are pre-aligned, assigned one of only three distributions, and split while sharing molecular identities across training and testing. This supports controlled recovery within known identities, but not broader real-world symmetry discovery. Molecular canonicalization improves accuracy only from 52.40% to 55.92%, versus 96.40% with augmentations reversed, recovering just 8% of the lost accuracy.
